claims.text: A hybrid ML–CALPHAD framework can predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase heat capacity for single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The hybrid framework can achieve less than approximately 5% prediction error across a wide HEA composition range.
Training on high-quality DSC, laser-melting, and in situ XRD data enables accurate prediction of HEA melting properties.
Appropriate annealing can minimize phase segregation and yield homogeneous, single-phase HEA ingots.
Dynamically incorporating new experimental datasets will refine the framework's thermodynamic predictions.
A controlled atmosphere near the melting point prevents oxidation and permits a stable solid-to-liquid transition.
XRD can be used to identify the phase composition and crystal structure of an HEA sample.
Verification of a uniform single-phase microstructure ensures that measured transition properties are intrinsic to alloy composition.
The ML component can rapidly screen vast compositional spaces.
CALPHAD imposes thermodynamic consistency by comparing Gibbs free energies and selecting the phase or phases with minimum Gibbs free energy.
Configurational entropy and mixing or formation enthalpy contribute to alloy phase stability through the Gibbs free energy.
Combining ML screening with CALPHAD constraints captures both configurational effects and physical constraints sufficiently to predict high-temperature transition properties.
CALPHAD descriptions can produce thermodynamic properties and phase diagrams that agree well with measurements.
Predictions will match experimental high-temperature thermodynamic properties within approximately 5% across diverse HEA compositions.
Existing DSC and laser-melting studies on HEAs have established reproducible melting data in single-phase alloys.
Existing HEA studies have used XRD and microstructural analysis to investigate phase structure stability after high-temperature annealing.
The framework is mainly applicable to homogeneous, single-phase HEAs and may not extend to multiphase alloys or compositions with extreme atomic-size mismatch.
Significant kinetic effects, metastable phases, segregation, or additional interphase interactions can limit predictive performance.
DSC, calorimetry, high-temperature XRD, and thermal analysis can jointly measure the target melting and liquid-state properties for validation.
The approach is falsified for its intended accuracy if errors exceed 5% for more than 70% of tested compositions.
